newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay shares weighed down by profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Bombay shares weighed down by profit-taking.

text.p: ** (0515 GMT) - Bombay stocks open lower, fall prey to
profit-booking on last day of weekly trade account
** Bombay's benchmark 30-share index down 17.15 pts at
3,856.70 in mid-morning trade, sluggish volumes
** Market seen consolidating at current levels with focus
on action of foreign funds, traders say
** Utility-maker Mahindra & Mahindra gains 4.25 rupees to
347.0 ahead of 1996/97 results due next week
** National exchange index falls 3.25 points at 1,083.35
Blue chips at Bombay exchanges drifted in mid-morning session on Friday, as the last day of the weekly account attracted profit-taking, traders said.
The market correction snapped a six-day winning streak in which the Bombay index has gained 189 points or five percent.
At 1120 (0550 GMT), Bombay's share index was trading 22.08 points, or 0.57 percent, lower at 3,851.77.
"We could see a topsy-turvy market today due to the end-account trade," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securites, the Indian associate of Goldman Sachs.
"But, there is no panic. We are seeing a correction."
A reaction in share prices was widely anticipated due to end-account considerations, but prices could firm up after a bout of profit-taking, participants said.
"The market is likely to show a correction, but there is some strength displayed in select stocks," said Deepak Mehta, chief trader at Reliance Capital Ltd.
Shares of tobacco conglomerate ITC crawled 0.75 rupees higher at 486.50 rupees, with over 5,03,00 shares traded at the Bombay exchange.
Truck-maker TELCO was unchaged at 404.0 rupees in volumes of 3,23,500 sahres.
"Investors appear to be adopting a wait-and-see attitude pending the expected announcement of an increase in petroleum products," Morgan Stanley said in its latest India strategy report.
The 15-party ruling United Front coalition's policy-setting steering committee is due to take a decision on hiking petroleum product prices on June 15.
Strong opposition from left-wing constituents of the United Front had prevented the committee from reaching a consensus on raising the prices of oil products at its last meeting on May 25.

"The degree of the increase and the type of products for which prices are raised should provide some indication of how serious the government is about reducing the fiscal deficit," Morgan Stanley said.

Analysts said the government must decide soon how to pay money owed to oil companies -- a total of 155 billion rupees ($4.33 billion) at the end of March -- for selling subsided petroleum products well below global prices.
The deficit is expected to rise to 245 billion rupees by March 31, 1998
-- Anshuman Daga, Bombay equities desk +91-22-265 9000
